It was strange, you know? I had lived on Earth my entire life. I never had any desire to visit any of the colonies in the system because Earth was just naturally alive. Mars was getting there, sure, but it would be hundreds of years before there would be enough domes to cover even a tenth of the red planet. But on Earth, we didn't need the domes. We didn't need the subterranean tunnels found in the dwarf planets of the belt, and we didn't need the space stations around Jupiter. Earth protected us from almost every danger.

Almost.

It was discovered quite accidentally, really. An astronomer was viewing a nearby star when, while he was viewing it, the star seemed to rip apart. It didn't explode. It didn't implode. It looked as if it became oblong for a few moments, then it faded away.

The astronomy community was, of course, very excited by this find. That is, until a few years later when they observed it happen again to a star that was much closer.

They called it BHSK-1. It was a black hole that was traveling nearly at a quarter of the speed of light, and swallowing up the previous star had set it on a trajectory straight for our solar system. It's mass was almost a thousand times that of the sun. None of us would survive.

Thankfully, we had almost ten years to prepare. We built huge ships on Earth. People from the colonies traveled inward to their mother planet to seek refuge from the coming monster. Most of their ships were decades old and wouldn't be able to make the journey into interstellar space.

Though none of my generation will ever see the new colonies that our decedents will build, it is enough to know that human kind will live on. Perhaps not where it originated, but out there, somewhere, future humans will populate until the end of time itself. For them, the galaxy awaits.
